canonical_statement: The study aims to improve critical error detection in failed long-horizon LLM-agent trajectories by identifying the earliest failure-responsible error step.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Critical error detection aims to locate the earliest error step in a failed trajectory that is responsible for the final failure.

canonical_statement: A decisive error is defined as a step whose replacement with a correct action, with all prior steps unchanged and the remainder allowed to unfold correctly, would have converted failure to success; the critical error step is the earliest decisive error.
TRAJDEBUG decomposes critical error detection into error trigger detection, error state classification, and critical attribution.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: TRAJDEBUG decomposes the task into three stages: error trigger detection, error state classification, and critical attribution.

canonical_statement: TRAJDEBUG uses multi-granularity history compression so local evidence can remain detailed while distant context is compressed.

For each trajectory step, TRAJDEBUG constructs high-detail, medium-detail, and low-detail views that progressively retain local evidence, main intent/state updates, and coarse progress with unresolved commitments.

Error triggers are treated as evidence-grounded mismatches between an erroneous commitment in the current step and a violated reference from the task, prior trajectory, environment feedback, or the same step.
TRAJDEBUG discards a candidate trigger unless both the erroneous commitment and the violated reference are explicitly citable as verbatim evidence.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: both q_w and q_r must be explicitly citable; otherwise, the trigger is discarded.

canonical_statement: Trigger reference categories are Task Conflict, History Conflict, Intra-Step Conflict, and Environment Anomaly.
Related triggers are clustered into one error instance when they violate the same reference object, so repeated manifestations of the same wrong commitment are not overcounted.
Each error instance is classified by whether the wrong commitment is resolved and whether it leaves an observable terminal footprint.
The four error states are Clean Resolution, Costly Resolution, Manifest Active, and Latent Active.
A terminal footprint is assigned for irreversible state change, a persistent semantic footprint, or budget debt; budget debt is operationalized as repair after more than 50% of the trajectory.
Only Costly Resolution and Manifest Active error instances are retained as terminal-relevant candidates for final attribution.
The final attribution stage uses an LLM to select the critical error from the retained candidates using each candidate's first step, state label, and supporting verbatim evidence.
The pilot study randomly sampled 50 failed trajectories from WhoAndWhen and AgentDebugBench, totaling 1,373 trajectory steps.

canonical_statement: The end-to-end τ²-Bench airline case study trajectory contained 49 steps; TRAJDEBUG detected 15 triggers, clustered them into 9 instances, and retained 4 candidate instances.
In the case study, TRAJDEBUG selected step 25 as the critical error, exactly matching the human annotation.
The implementation uses compression limits of up to 3,000 characters for high-detail views, 1,200 for medium-detail views, and 600 for low-detail views.
Budget debt is checked with a Python script by testing whether the distance from origin step to repair step exceeds 50% of trajectory length.
Direct-prompting baselines truncate each trajectory step to 2,048 characters and use a maximum context length of 16,384 tokens.
The authors conclude that TRAJDEBUG outperforms LLM prompting and diagnostic baselines and that its diagnoses can support trajectory repair and transferable failure memory.
The authors position critical error detection as a promising interface for inference-time agent improvement.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: These results position critical error detection as a promising interface for inference-time agent improvement.

canonical_statement: TRAJDEBUG still relies on LLMs for error interpretation and final attribution, so predictions may depend on model reasoning ability, domain knowledge, and calibration.
Because TRAJDEBUG is staged, false negatives in trigger detection or state classification can cause the final candidate set to omit the true critical error.
The authors advise manual verification of important TRAJDEBUG diagnoses before use in high-stakes settings because the framework can make incorrect predictions.
The authors state that TRAJDEBUG, its associated code, and TRAJERRBENCH will be released under the MIT license.
